183.title: One in a thousand (7.1–7.12)
183.hook: chapter seven opens with a sobering number, and then strings the whole world on a thread
183.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant Om at the start of prayer or study, and the image of the world strung on the divine like pearls on a thread (Gita 7.7) is a common teaching of God's presence in all things.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one who fell short, and the kindest answer in the Gita. Your line was nothing is lost. Did you pick one dropped thing back up? Today, chapter seven begins. Day one hundred eighty-three.
screen: `THE ONE WHO FELL SHORT — NOTHING IS LOST.`

segments.voice: A pearl necklace breaks, and the pearls scatter across the floor. For a second you see what was hidden the whole time. It wasn't just a row of pearls. There was a thread running through every one of them, holding the shape. You never noticed the thread, because the pearls were the pretty part. Chapter seven of the Gita starts a new section, and it opens with two things. A sobering number about how rare real understanding is. And then this very picture: the whole world, strung like pearls on a thread you can't see.
screen: `A NECKLACE BREAKS.` → `THE THREAD WAS THERE ALL ALONG.` → `CHAPTER SEVEN BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Krishna opens by promising something complete. Listen, and you'll know me fully, he says, with knowledge and with realization, jnana and vijnana, knowing about and knowing through experience. And then the number, verse three. Among thousands of people, one strives for perfection. And among those who strive and succeed, scarcely one knows me as I really am. One in a thousand, and then one in a thousand of those. It's not a threat. It's honesty about how hard this is, and a quiet dignity for anyone who's trying at all. Then he describes how the world is made. There's his lower nature, eightfold: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, and the sense of I. That's everything you can point to, including your own thoughts. And there's his higher nature, the life in things, which holds the whole world up. From these two, all beings come, and Krishna is the source and the end of the whole universe. Then verse seven, the necklace. There is nothing higher than me, Arjuna. All this is strung on me, like pearls on a thread. And he starts listing where the thread shows. I am the light of the sun and the moon. The sacred syllable Om in all the Vedas. The sound in space. The sweet fragrance of the earth. The strength of the strong, free of craving. We'll hear more of that list later in the Gita. That's today's word: one in a thousand. Rare to see the thread. But it runs through every pearl.
screen: `KNOWLEDGE AND REALIZATION.` · `ONE IN A THOUSAND.` · `LOWER AND HIGHER NATURE.` · `PEARLS ON A THREAD.` · then, large: `RARE TO SEE. EVERYWHERE PRESENT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and count through the eight of the lower nature, slowly, one per breath. Earth: the weight of your body on the seat. Water: the wet of your mouth. Fire: the warmth of your hands. Air: the breath itself. Space: the room around you. Mind: the thoughts passing. Intellect: the part that's following along. And the sense of I, the one sitting here. Then, for the rest of the time, rest on whatever holds all eight together. The bell holds the time.
One in a thousand. Gita seven, three: among thousands, one strives, and among those, scarcely one knows the truth. Rare, and still strung through everything.
screen: `ONE IN A THOUSAND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: rare. Today, notice one ordinary thing, the light, a smell of the earth after rain, and imagine the thread running through it. Day one hundred eighty-three.

184.title: Four kinds of devotees (7.13–7.19)
184.hook: people come to God in trouble, in curiosity, in need, and in knowing; the Gita calls all four noble
184.howItsDone: Hindu temples welcome people who come for every reason: prayers in illness or trouble, questions, requests for success or a good year, and daily worship with no request at all; Gita 7.16 is often cited to honor all of them.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: one in a thousand, and the world strung like pearls on a thread. Your line was rare. Did you catch the thread in anything ordinary? Day one hundred eighty-four.
screen: `ONE IN A THOUSAND — RARE.`

segments.voice: Walk into a temple on any evening and look at the faces. A mother whose son is in the hospital. A student the night before an exam. A man whose shop isn't doing well, asking for a better year. A teenager who's just curious what all this is. An old woman who's been coming every day for sixty years and doesn't seem to need anything at all. Some people might say only one of them is here for the right reason. The Gita, chapter seven, looks at the same crowd, and says something more generous.
screen: `A MOTHER. A STUDENT. A SHOPKEEPER.` → `A CURIOUS TEENAGER.` → `SIXTY YEARS OF EVENINGS.`

segments.voice: First, the problem. The world is bewildered by the three gunas, Krishna says, the three strands of nature, and so it doesn't see him beyond them. His power of illusion is hard to cross, but those who turn to him cross it. Then verse sixteen. Four kinds of good people turn to me, Arjuna. The arta: the one in distress. The jijnasu: the one who wants to know. The artharthi: the one who seeks something, wealth, security, a good outcome. And the jnani: the one who knows. That's the mother, the teenager, the shopkeeper, and the old woman. Here's what's striking. All four are called good people, and verse eighteen calls all of them noble: udara, generous, large-hearted. Nobody gets turned away for coming in trouble or coming with a request. But one stands out. The one who knows, verse seventeen says, always united, devoted to one alone, is the best. I am very dear to that one, and that one is dear to me. Verse eighteen goes further: the one who knows is my very self. And verse nineteen describes the journey there. At the end of many births, the one who knows takes refuge in me, seeing that Vasudeva is everything. Such a great soul, Krishna says, is very hard to find. So the ladder isn't a test you pass or fail. You can come in scared. You can come in curious. You can come asking for a job. The door is open. And the Gita keeps walking you toward the fourth. That's today's word: four kinds of devotees.
screen: `THE ONE IN DISTRESS.` · `THE ONE WHO WANTS TO KNOW.` · `THE ONE WHO SEEKS SOMETHING.` · `THE ONE WHO KNOWS.` · then, large: `ALL FOUR ARE NOBLE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask yourself honestly which of the four you are today. Are you here in some kind of trouble? Out of curiosity? Wanting something to change? Or just to be here? There's no wrong answer; the Gita calls all four noble. Breathe with whatever you found. Then, for the last part of the sit, let the reason go, and simply sit, as the one who doesn't need anything. The bell holds the time.
Four kinds of devotees: the one in distress, the one who wants to know, the one who seeks something, and the one who knows. All four noble.
screen: `FOUR KINDS OF DEVOTEES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the one who knows. Today, notice why you reach for something bigger than you, and don't be embarrassed by the reason. Day one hundred eighty-four.

185.title: Maya and the veil (7.20–7.30)
185.hook: Krishna says he is hidden in plain sight, covered by his own maya
185.howItsDone: Hindu schools understand maya in different ways: Advaita Vedanta teaches it as the appearance of the one reality as many, while Vaishnava schools teach it as the Lord's real power; many Hindus speak of maya when describing the pull of worldly wanting.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: four kinds of devotees, the one in distress, the curious, the one who asks, and the one who knows. Your line was the one who knows. Day one hundred eighty-five, the last day of chapter seven.
screen: `FOUR KINDS OF DEVOTEES — THE ONE WHO KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Have you ever watched a great magic show up close? The magician is right there, three feet away, sleeves rolled up. Nothing's hidden. And you still can't see how it's done. The trick isn't that the magician is behind a curtain. It's that you're looking exactly where the magician wants you to look. That's close to one of the oldest meanings of a Sanskrit word you've probably heard: maya. People translate it illusion. But in the Gita, Krishna uses it about himself. He says he's right here, and hidden, covered by his own maya.
screen: `THREE FEET AWAY. NOTHING HIDDEN.` → `STILL YOU CAN'T SEE IT.` → `MAYA.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-five: I am not revealed to everyone, veiled by my yoga-maya. This confused world doesn't recognize me, unborn and unchanging. In the oldest Sanskrit, maya meant something like wondrous power, the skill of a god to make forms appear. Only later did it come to be heard mostly as illusion. And Hindu schools read it differently. In Advaita Vedanta, maya is the power by which the one reality appears as many; the world isn't ultimately what it seems. In devotional schools like those of Ramanuja and Madhva, the world is real, and maya is the Lord's real power, which can both reveal and hide. Either way, the veil is his. Around it, these verses say something generous and something hard. Generous: verses twenty-one and twenty-two. Whatever form a devotee wants to worship with faith, I make that faith steady, and what they receive, they receive from me. Hard: verse twenty-four. People who don't understand think the unseen has simply become something seen, without knowing the higher, unchanging nature behind it. And verse twenty-seven names what does the veiling inside us: the pair of wanting and not-wanting. From birth, everyone is caught in that push and pull. Those who come out of it, verse twenty-eight says, worship steadily. And the chapter ends by naming words the next chapter will explain: Brahman, the self, action, and more. That's the word today, maya and the veil. What's behind it isn't far away. It's covered.
screen: `HIDDEN BY MY OWN MAYA.` · `WONDROUS POWER, THEN ILLUSION.` · `WHATEVER FORM, I MAKE FAITH STEADY.` · `THE VEIL OF WANTING AND NOT-WANTING.` · then, large: `NOT FAR. COVERED.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-seven says the veil is woven of liking and disliking. So sit, and watch the weaving. Each time something comes up, a sound, a memory, an itch, notice whether you lean toward it or away. Just label it silently: like, dislike, like. Don't change anything. After a while, see if there's a moment between the like and the dislike, a thin gap where nothing's being pulled. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Maya and the veil. In the Gita, maya is Krishna's own power, which hides him in plain sight. The veil is woven from wanting and not-wanting.
screen: `MAYA AND THE VEIL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: behind the veil. Today, when a strong like or dislike grabs you, pause, and ask what it might be covering. Day one hundred eighty-five.

186.title: What is Brahman? (8.1–8.7)
186.hook: Arjuna fires off seven questions in a row, and the last one is about the moment of death
186.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice smarana, the constant remembering of God, by repeating a divine name through the day, and families often chant God's name at the bedside of someone who is dying, in the spirit of Gita 8.5–8.7.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: maya and the veil, the power that hides Krishna in plain sight. Your line was behind the veil. Chapter seven ended with a handful of big words. Today, Arjuna asks what they mean. Day one hundred eighty-six.
screen: `MAYA AND THE VEIL — BEHIND THE VEIL.`

segments.voice: You know that moment in a class when the teacher uses five words you don't know in one sentence, and everyone else nods, and you finally raise your hand? That's Arjuna at the start of chapter eight. Krishna has just dropped a string of big terms. Brahman. The self. Action. And Arjuna doesn't nod. He asks, one after another: What is Brahman? What is the self? What is action? And then the question underneath all the others: at the time of death, how are you known?
screen: `FIVE WORDS YOU DON'T KNOW.` → `ARJUNA RAISES HIS HAND.` → `SEVEN QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Krishna answers them fast, one line each. Brahman, verse three, is the imperishable, the highest. The word akshara, imperishable, also means a syllable, a letter, something that can't be broken down further. The self, adhyatma, is one's own essential nature. Action, karma, is the creative outpouring that brings beings into existence. Then the perishable world of things, the cosmic person behind the gods, and, the Lord of sacrifice: Krishna himself, here, in this body. That's the dictionary. But then comes the part people remember. Verse five: whoever, at the time of the end, leaves the body remembering me alone, comes to my being. There's no doubt about it. And verse six widens it: whatever state a person remembers at the end, as they leave the body, to that state they go, because they've always been shaped by it. So the moment of death isn't a pop quiz. It's the sum of what you've been practicing all along. Which is why verse seven, the closing line of this section, is so practical. Therefore, at all times, remember me, and fight. Remember, and fight. Not remember instead of living; remember while living. Arjuna is still standing between two armies. Krishna doesn't tell him to go meditate in a cave until he dies. He says: keep me in mind, and do what's in front of you. That's the word today, what is Brahman? The imperishable. And the practical answer: remember, in the middle of everything.
screen: `SEVEN QUESTIONS.` · `BRAHMAN: THE IMPERISHABLE.` · `WHAT YOU REMEMBER AT THE END.` · `AT ALL TIMES, REMEMBER, AND FIGHT.` · then, large: `REMEMBER, WHILE LIVING.`

segments.voice: Verse six says we become what we're shaped by. So sit, and look at what you've been remembering lately. What comes to mind most often, when your mind is free? A worry, a person, a screen? Don't judge it. Then choose one thing you'd like to be shaped by: a name of God if you pray, a person you love, a line from this path. Return to it on every breath. The bell holds the time.
What is Brahman? Arjuna's first question. Krishna's answer: the imperishable, the highest. And then: remember me at all times.
screen: `WHAT IS BRAHMAN? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: remember me. Three times today, in the middle of something, bring to mind the one thing you chose, and keep going. Day one hundred eighty-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: Brahman is a caste.
what it means: Brahman is the imperishable, the highest reality; and the way to it is to remember, at all times.

what a scholar hears: Brahman (neuter, the absolute) is a different word from Brahma (the creator god) and brahmana (priest); 8.3 defines it as akshara, and 8.6 grounds the 'last thought' in a lifetime's bhava.

187.title: The last thought (8.8–8.16)
187.hook: a king gave up his throne to meditate, then spent his last breath thinking about a baby deer
187.carry: what you think at the end
187.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant Om or a divine name daily so that it will come naturally at the end, and families often recite God's name, or play recorded chanting, for a dying relative.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: what is Brahman? The imperishable. And a practical answer: at all times, remember. Your line was remember me. Did the thing you chose come back to you during the day? Day one hundred eighty-seven.
screen: `WHAT IS BRAHMAN? — REMEMBER ME.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells of a king named Bharata who gave up his kingdom and went to live by a river in the forest, to spend his days in prayer. One day a pregnant deer, frightened by a lion's roar, leapt the river, gave birth, and died. The fawn was left alone. Bharata took it in. He fed it, worried about it, went looking for it when it wandered. Little by little the fawn filled his whole mind. And when Bharata died, the story says, the last thing he was thinking about was the deer. Hold on to that story. Today's verses are why it's told.
screen: `A KING IN THE FOREST.` → `AN ORPHANED FAWN.` → `HIS LAST THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: In the story, Bharata is reborn as a deer. It's not a punishment. It's the Gita's teaching made into a picture: what fills your mind shapes where you go. The story goes on; he keeps the memory of his past life, and in his next birth he finally reaches the goal. Chapter eight, verses eight to sixteen, describe the other way to die. Meditate on the ancient seer, the ruler, finer than the finest, who holds everything up, whose form can't be imagined, bright as the sun beyond darkness. At the time of departure, verse ten says, with a steady mind and devotion, draw the breath up between the brows. Verse thirteen gives the single syllable to hold: speaking Om, which is Brahman, and remembering Krishna, the one who leaves the body goes to the highest goal. Then verse fourteen, and here's the gentleness. For the one who always remembers me, every day, with a mind that goes nowhere else, I am easy to reach. Sulabha: easily attained. The great souls who come to Krishna, verse fifteen says, don't come back to this temporary home of sorrow. So the last thought isn't really about the last moment. You can't cram for it. Bharata had given up everything else, and a fawn still filled his mind, because it's what he'd thought about every day. The last thought is made of all the ordinary ones. That's today's word. Your last thought is being written now, one day at a time.
screen: `WHAT FILLS THE MIND SHAPES WHERE YOU GO.` · `OM, AND THE BREATH BETWEEN THE BROWS.` · `EASY TO REACH, FOR THE ONE WHO REMEMBERS.` · `YOU CAN'T CRAM FOR IT.` · then, large: `THE LAST THOUGHT IS BEING WRITTEN NOW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let today's ordinary thoughts pass by like a slideshow: the morning, the commute, the people, the screens. Just watch which ones keep coming back. Those are the ones being practiced. Then, if you're comfortable with it, hum a long, quiet Om on the out-breath, or simply let the breath out slowly, and rest in the silence after it. Do that a few times. The bell holds the time.
The last thought. Gita chapter eight: what you remember at the end is what you've been remembering all along, and for the one who always remembers, God is easy to reach.
screen: `THE LAST THOUGHT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what you think at the end. Today, notice which thought you've practiced most. Is it one you'd want at the end? Day one hundred eighty-seven.

188.title: Day and night of Brahma (8.17–8.28)
188.hook: a single day of the creator lasts a thousand ages, and the universe breathes in and out with it
188.tomorrow: "I will tell you the most secret" (9.1–9.10)
188.howItsDone: Many Hindus consider uttarayana, the sun's northern course marked by the festival of Makar Sankranti, an auspicious time, and the Mahabharata's Bhishma is remembered for waiting for it before he died.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last thought, and a king who died thinking of a fawn. Your line was what you think at the end. Today, the biggest clock in the Gita. Day one hundred eighty-eight, the end of chapter eight.
screen: `THE LAST THOUGHT — WHAT YOU THINK AT THE END.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata, the great elder Bhishma falls in battle, pierced by so many arrows that his body rests on them like a bed. And he doesn't die. He had been given the power to choose his time. So he lies there, on the arrows, for days, teaching, waiting. Waiting for what? For the sun to turn north: uttarayana, the half of the year when the days grow longer. Only then does he let go. Why would the direction of the sun matter at the moment of death? Today's verses, the end of chapter eight, are where that idea lives.
screen: `A BED OF ARROWS.` → `BHISHMA WAITS.` → `FOR THE SUN TO TURN NORTH.`

segments.voice: First, the enormous clock. Verse seventeen: those who know that a day of Brahma, the creator, lasts a thousand ages, and his night another thousand, truly know day and night. When Brahma's day dawns, all things come out of the unmanifest. When his night falls, they dissolve back into it. Verse nineteen: the same crowd of beings, born again and again, dissolves at nightfall, helplessly, and comes forth again at day. The whole universe breathing in and out. Later texts even did the arithmetic, and a day of Brahma comes out in the billions of years. But, verse twenty, beyond that unmanifest there's another unmanifest, eternal, which doesn't perish when all beings perish. That's the highest goal; whoever reaches it doesn't return. And then the two paths. Verses twenty-four and twenty-five. One path: fire, light, day, the bright half of the moon, the six months of the sun's northern course. The knowers of Brahman who go by it reach Brahman. The other: smoke, night, the dark half of the moon, the six months of the southern course. Those who go by it reach the light of the moon, and return. Commentators read this differently. Some take it as the actual timing of death; that's how Bhishma read it. Others read the markers as guides or stages on the soul's journey, the path of light and the path of smoke. Verse twenty-seven is clear either way: the yogi who knows these two paths isn't confused. That's today's word, the day and night of Brahma. A clock so large it holds the universe, and something beyond it that no clock touches.
screen: `A THOUSAND AGES FOR A DAY.` · `THE UNIVERSE BREATHES IN AND OUT.` · `BEYOND IT, WHAT NEVER PERISHES.` · `THE PATH OF LIGHT, THE PATH OF SMOKE.` · then, large: `THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath become a very small version of Brahma's day and night. On the in-breath, let things come forth: sounds, thoughts, the feel of the room. On the out-breath, let them all dissolve back into quiet. In, the world appears. Out, it rests. Then, for the last few breaths, notice what doesn't come and go: the awareness watching both. The bell holds the time.
Day and night of Brahma. A thousand ages each: the universe coming forth and dissolving, and beyond it, the eternal that never perishes.

189.title: "I will tell you the most secret" (9.1–9.10)
189.word: "I will tell you the most secret
189.hook: Krishna promises the royal secret, and it turns out to be a riddle about where the world lives
189.tomorrow: The one who offers a leaf (9.11–9.25)
189.howItsDone: Chapter nine, the raja-vidya raja-guhya yoga, is one of the most loved chapters of the Gita; many Hindus read it for its teaching that all beings rest in God and that devotion is easy and open to all.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the day and night of Brahma, and the path of light and the path of smoke. Your line was the two paths. Day one hundred eighty-nine, the end of the week, and the start of chapter nine.
screen: `DAY AND NIGHT OF BRAHMA — THE TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Look at the week behind you. One in a thousand, and the world strung like pearls on a thread. Four kinds of devotees, all noble. Maya, the veil. What is Brahman, and remember me. The last thought. The day and night of Brahma. It's been a week of big ideas. And now Krishna leans in, the way a friend does when the room goes quiet, and says: I'm going to tell you the most secret thing. Because you don't sneer. Everybody leans in for a secret. So what is it?
screen: `A WEEK OF BIG IDEAS.` → `THE ROOM GOES QUIET.` → `THE MOST SECRET THING.`

segments.voice: Verse one: to you, who doesn't find fault, I'll tell the most secret knowledge, together with its realization. Verse two gives it a grand name: raja-vidya, raja-guhya. The king of knowledge, the king of secrets. The highest purifier. And then three surprising words. It's known directly, by experience. It's in line with dharma. And it's easy to practice. The deepest secret in the Gita is called easy. Here it is. Verse four: all this world is pervaded by me, in my unseen form. All beings rest in me. But I don't rest in them. Then verse five turns it over: and yet, beings don't rest in me either. Behold my divine power. It's a riddle, on purpose. Verse six gives a picture to hold it. As the great wind, moving everywhere, always rests in space, so all beings rest in me. The wind moves; space doesn't. The wind is in space, but space isn't pushed around by the wind, and it isn't used up by it. So everything is in Krishna, and nothing contains or disturbs him. Then the cycle from yesterday comes back. At the end of an age all beings go into my nature, and at the beginning, I send them forth again. And those actions don't bind me, verse nine says: I sit as if unconcerned, unattached. Verse ten: under my eye, nature brings forth the moving and the unmoving, and the world turns. That's the royal secret, as the Gita tells it: you're already inside the one you're looking for, like wind inside the sky.
screen: `THE KING OF SECRETS.` · `KNOWN DIRECTLY, EASY TO PRACTICE.` · `ALL BEINGS REST IN ME.` · `LIKE WIND IN THE SKY.` · then, large: `YOU'RE ALREADY INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and imagine a wide, open sky. Now feel the wind moving through it, gusts and eddies, some strong, some gentle. Let your thoughts be the wind. Let the sky be whatever holds them. The wind moves; the sky doesn't mind. Each time a thought gusts through, notice the space it's moving in. You don't need to stop the wind. Just rest as the sky. The bell holds the time.
I will tell you the most secret. Gita nine: the king of secrets is that all beings rest in God, as wind rests in the sky.

original.note: Sanskrit: raja-guhya, the royal secret; guhya, secret, from guh, to hide.

trapdoor: what you thought: a secret means something hidden from most people.
what it means: the king of secrets is right in front of you, known directly and easy to practice: all beings rest in God, like wind in the sky.

what a scholar hears: guhya comes from guh, to hide, the root of guha, a cave; 9.4–5's paradox (beings are in me, yet not in me) is called 'my divine yoga', and the wind-in-space image of 9.6 is how the Gita resolves it.
